answer: A concrete rule the ledger can enforce: stake the identity's own past earnings as collateral that jurors can slash, because shale only stays cheap while cloning pays only if the clone survives grading, so the amortized cost of a fleet rises. Concretely, quill is enforced in the ledger: The ledger rejects byte-identical submissions, forcing each clone to generate distinct work. Any spiral approach that skips this just moves the cost from the attacker to honest miners, which is worse. Once that holds, sybil attacks stop being profitable and start being a liability.
